title: NVIDIA Launches Preset C DLSS Frame Generation, Boosting Speed Up to 35% – TechPowerUp
body:
NVIDIA has rolled out a new performance preset for its DLSS Frame Generation technology, promising up to a 35 percent boost in frame‑creation speed. Branded “Preset C,” the update arrives as part of today’s beta release of the NVIDIA Control Panel app and targets GeForce RTX 40‑series, the upcoming RTX 50‑series, and RTX Spark‑enabled laptops. By tightening the algorithm’s latency and computational load, the company claims gamers will see smoother motion and higher frame rates without sacrificing the visual fidelity that AI‑upscaled rendering is known for.

The enhancement builds on the company’s broader DLSS roadmap, which has evolved from a simple upscaling tool into a full‑fledged AI‑driven frame synthesis pipeline. Since the debut of DLSS 2.0, NVIDIA has leveraged deep learning super‑sampling to reconstruct high‑resolution images from lower‑resolution inputs, freeing GPU cycles for higher frame rates. Frame Generation, introduced with DLSS 3, adds an extra layer: the AI engine predicts intermediate frames, effectively doubling the perceived refresh rate. However, this process has historically required a noticeable share of the GPU’s tensor cores, leading to a trade‑off between speed and power consumption. Preset C aims to tip the balance in favor of speed, delivering the fastest possible generation mode while keeping power draw within acceptable limits for both desktop and mobile platforms.

Early benchmarks shared by NVIDIA show that the new preset can shave roughly one‑third of the time required to generate each AI frame compared with the previous “Performance” mode. In practical terms, a game running at 60 fps with DLSS 3 could climb to the mid‑70s or even approach 80 fps on an RTX 4090, while a laptop equipped with an RTX 4070 Laptop GPU could see a similar uplift without overheating. The company attributes the gain to a refined tensor‑core scheduling algorithm and a leaner neural network architecture that reduces the number of inference steps per frame. By pruning redundant calculations, the model maintains comparable visual quality, according to side‑by‑side comparisons released alongside the update.

Industry analysts see the move as a strategic response to growing competition in the AI‑enhanced graphics space. AMD’s FidelityFX Super Resolution 2 (FSR 2) and Intel’s XeSS have both introduced frame‑generation variants, but neither has matched NVIDIA’s integration depth or the sheer raw performance of its tensor cores. The introduction of a faster preset could cement NVIDIA’s lead among high‑end gamers and content creators who rely on real‑time rendering for immersive experiences, such as VR and cloud‑gaming services. Moreover, the update arrives just as the company prepares to launch the RTX 50‑series, suggesting that the new hardware will be optimized for the accelerated workflow, potentially unlocking even greater gains.

Critics, however, caution that faster frame generation may come at the cost of increased power consumption and heat output, especially on thin‑and‑light laptops. While NVIDIA assures that Preset C respects thermal envelopes, real‑world testing will be essential to verify these claims across a range of chassis designs. Additionally, the beta nature of the rollout means that stability and compatibility with older titles remain unproven. Some developers have reported visual artifacts when DLSS 3 is pushed to its limits, and a more aggressive preset could exacerbate such issues unless game‑specific tuning is applied.

Looking ahead, the introduction of Preset C signals NVIDIA’s commitment to refining AI‑driven rendering as a core pillar of its GPU strategy. As the ecosystem of games and professional applications increasingly adopts DLSS‑compatible pipelines, further optimizations—such as adaptive preset switching based on workload or dynamic power budgeting—could become standard features. For gamers, the promise of higher frame rates without sacrificing image quality may translate into more fluid competitive play and richer cinematic experiences. For the broader industry, the push toward faster, more efficient frame generation underscores the growing importance of AI in real‑time graphics, a trend that is likely to shape the next generation of visual computing.
